segments.english: Then there was set before him to eat. He said, "I will not eat until I have spoken my words." Then he said, "Speak."
segments.literal: and-was-set to-faces-of-him to-eat and-said not I-eat until if I-spoke my-words and-said speak

tokens.note: Hofal (passive) of שׂוּם, the doer not named. The qere form is translated; the ketiv is in the apparatus.
לְפָנָיו, lit. 'to his faces': the idiom 'before him'.
Infinitive construct with ל: the purpose of the setting.
Yiqtol 1cs with לֹא: 'I will not eat'.
עַד of time.
אִם here has the force of כִּי, as Rashi says; with עַד the pair means 'until'. The English 'until' carries both tokens.
Piel perfect 1cs: the speaking is complete before the eating.
Plural דְּבָרִים with the 1cs suffix.
Piel imperative 2ms.

phrases.english: Then there was set before him to eat
phrases.literal: and-was-set to-faces-of-him to-eat: the hofal has no named doer, so the English passive has none; 'there was' is the English form of the unnamed passive.
and-said not I-eat: the negative with the yiqtol makes the refusal.

phrases.english: until I have spoken my words
phrases.literal: until if I-spoke my-words: 'until that I spoke my words'; the perfect is completed before the eating.
and-said speak: the speaker of 'speak' is not named in the Hebrew, so the English keeps 'he'.

grammar: הוּשַׂם is the hofal of שׂוּם, a passive in the wayyiqtol; the Hebrew names no doer, and the English passive keeps that.
The infinitive לֶאֱכֹל gives the purpose of the setting; the negative לֹא אֹכַל is the refusal, and the qatal דִּבַּרְתִּי in the clause after עַד אִם is completed before the eating.
The second וַיֹּאמֶר introduces the imperative דַּבֵּר; the speaker changes without a name in the Hebrew.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra (normative) reads the hofal as the binyan in which the doer is not named; the English follows him. Radak's servants and his name for the second speaker are recorded, not adopted.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: this is the binyan in which the name of the doer is not mentioned, as in ויושב את משה; the English therefore gives an unnamed passive.
Rashi: אִם here is used in the sense of כִּי, as in עַד כִּי יָבֹא שִׁילֹה; the sages count four senses of that particle, and one of them is אִם. The English reads 'until'.
Radak: the ketiv ויישם is taken from the root ישם; he sets the ketiv beside the form read here.
Radak: the form is hofal, and the food was set before him by the servants of the house; the Hebrew names no servants, so the English does not add them.
Radak: the one who says 'speak' is Laban or Bethuel; the Hebrew names neither, so the English keeps 'he'.

apparatus: Ketiv ויישם; qere וַיּוּשַׂם, the form translated. Radak takes the ketiv from the root ישם.

tokens.note: Construct with the following name: 'the servant of Abraham'.
The independent pronoun is the subject of a verbless sentence; 'am' is English for the equation.

phrases.literal: and-said servant-of Abraham I: a verbless sentence, the pronoun as subject and the construct noun as predicate; 'am' is supplied by English.

grammar: The verse is verbless after the verb of saying: 'servant of Abraham I', with the pronoun אָנֹכִי as subject; the English supplies 'am'.
The etnaḥta on וַיֹּאמַר divides the verse; the speech it opens runs on to 24:49 and is left open in this unit.
The servant is not named in this verse.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra (normative) rules that the words stand as their plain sense, not joined to the words about food. The English gives the plain sense.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: some take 'I am Abraham's servant' with the words about eating, so that some foods are forbidden to them; the correct reading is that his words stand in their plain meaning.

Radak: the Sages say that he first wished to be understood as only the servant of Abraham, the brother of his hearers, so that the honour they see is not his; a comment on his motive, not on the words.

segments.english: The LORD blessed my master greatly, and he became great; and he gave him flocks and cattle and silver and gold and servants and maidservants and camels and donkeys.
segments.literal: and-the-LORD blessed OBJ my-master greatly and-became-great and-gave to-him flocks and-cattle and-silver and-gold and-servants and-maidservants and-camels and-donkeys

tokens.note: יְהוָה, written here with the vowels of יְהֹוָה (see apparatus).
Piel perfect 3ms with God as subject: 'God blesses'.
The object marker has no English counterpart.
Adverb with the verb of blessing.
Wayyiqtol 3ms: the subject is the master.
Wayyiqtol 3ms; the giver is not named.
Silver as a costly gift.
Gold as a costly gift.
Plural of עֶבֶד.
Camel as property.

phrases.english: The LORD blessed my master greatly
phrases.literal: and-the-LORD blessed OBJ my-master greatly: the prefix ו has no English; the object marker is not translated.
and-became-great: the wayyiqtol continues the sequence after the qatal of blessing.
and-gave to-him: the giver is not named; 'he' keeps the 3ms form.

phrases.english: flocks and cattle and silver and gold and servants and maidservants and camels and donkeys
phrases.literal: flocks and-cattle and-silver and-gold and-servants and-maidservants and-camels and-donkeys: a list of eight with ו on each item after the first.

grammar: The qatal בֵּרַךְ opens the verse; the two wayyiqtol verbs carry the narrative on.
The subject of וַיִּגְדָּל and of וַיִּתֶּן is not stated; the Hebrew does not say whether the giver is the LORD or the master, and the English keeps 'he'.
The list is a run of nouns each with ו, the first without; the English 'and' follows the Hebrew.
segments.note: The three finite verbs have no named subject for the last two; the English keeps 'he'.

commentary.summary: Radak: the blessing was so great that his servant goes in great honour, as they see; this describes the effect and does not change the sense of מְאֹד.
Sforno: without doubt many in the land were eager to marry their daughters to his son; a comment on motive, not on the words.

apparatus: Vowels: WLC reads וַיהוָה for וַיהֹוָה; no change of sense.
context: Silver (כֶּסֶף) here is wealth given by weight, not coinage; coined money is much later than the patriarchal period.
The date at which camels came into use as beasts of burden in the region is disputed; the English gives 'camels' without a date.

segments.english: Sarah, my master's wife, bore a son to my master in her old age, and he gave him all that was his.
segments.literal: and-bore Sarah wife-of my-master son to-my-master after her-old-age and-gave to-him OBJ all that to-him

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol 3fs: the subject is Sarah.
Construct: 'the wife of my master'.
לַ dative with the name.
Time sense; the English renders 'in her old age' for the idiom.
Wayyiqtol 3ms; the giver is not named.
Suffix on לוֹ.
No English counterpart.
כֹּל, limited by the context to the things just mentioned.
לוֹ in the relative clause, 'that to him'; 'was' is English.

phrases.literal: and-bore Sarah wife-of my-master: the English puts 'my master's wife' after the name.
son: the object of 'bore'.

phrases.english: to my master in her old age
phrases.literal: to-my-master after her-old-age: 'after' in the time sense, English 'in'.
and-gave to-him: the giver is not named.
OBJ all that to-him: the relative clause has no verb; 'was' is English.

grammar: The verse is a run of wayyiqtol and noun phrases; the gender of the first verb agrees with Sarah.
אֵשֶׁת אֲדֹנִי is a construct chain: 'the wife of my master'.
אַחֲרֵי זִקְנָתָהּ has no verb: 'after her old age'; the English idiom is 'in her old age'.
segments.note: The copula in 'all that was his' is English; the Hebrew has only לוֹ.

commentary.summary: Rashi: he showed them the deed of gift; an account of how the giving was done, not of the words.
Radak: though he had a son by another woman, he gave all to Isaac out of love for Sarah his kinswoman and for Isaac; a comment on motive.
Sforno: therefore Isaac was dear to him from the time of his birth; a comment on the phrase 'in her old age'.

apparatus: Vowels: WLC reads לּוֹ for לוֹ; no change of sense.

segments.english: My master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell.'
segments.literal: and-made-swear-me my-master saying not you-take wife for-my-son from-daughters-of the-Canaanite who I dwelling in-his-land

tokens.note: Hiphil wayyiqtol 3ms with the 1cs suffix.
Infinitive construct לֵאמֹר introduces the speech.
Yiqtol 2ms with לֹא: a prohibition, 'you shall not take'.
The article with the gentilic is collective; the English uses the plural for it.
Participle: a present state, 'I dwell'.
The suffix refers to the Canaanites.

phrases.literal: and-made-swear-me my-master: the Hiphil with suffix; the English puts the subject first.
saying not you-take: the infinitive introduces the words; the yiqtol with לֹא is a prohibition.
a wife: the object of the prohibition.
for-my-son: the beneficiary.

phrases.english: from the daughters of the Canaanites
phrases.literal: from-daughters-of the-Canaanite: the gentilic is collective, so the English is plural.
who I dwelling in-his-land: a participle, 'I dwell', with the relative 'whose' for the people.

grammar: לֵאמֹר with the infinitive introduces the words; the English puts Abraham's words in single quotes inside the servant's speech.
לֹא תִקַּח is a yiqtol with לֹא: the prohibition 'you shall not take', addressed to the servant.
אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי יֹשֵׁב בְּאַרְצוֹ is a participle, 'I dwell in his land'; the suffix refers to the Canaanites.
segments.note: Single quotes mark Abraham's words inside the servant's speech; the outer double quotation is left open.

commentary.summary: Rashi reads the prohibition as conditional: 'if you do not first go to my father's house and do not agree to go after me'. The words state no condition, so the English keeps the plain prohibition.
Radak: the answer to 'why did you come so far' is that Abraham found a wife for his son among the great men of that land but would take only from his kin; a comment on motive.
Sforno: in the servant's words, since Abraham rejected the men of his land and chose his kin, the servant came to them; not because the land lacked women. A comment on motive.

segments.english: If not, you shall go to my father's house and to my kin, and take a wife for my son.
segments.literal: if not to house-of my-father you-go and-to my-clan and-you-take wife for-my-son

tokens.note: אִם with לֹא: 'if not', the alternative to the prohibition.
בֵּית אָבִי: the household as a family group.
Yiqtol 2ms.
מִשְׁפָּחָה: the clan.
Weqatal 2ms: continues the yiqtol of 'you shall go'.

phrases.literal: if not: the alternative to the prohibition in 24:37.

phrases.english: you shall go to my father's house
phrases.literal: to house-of my-father you-go: 'house of my father' is the English 'my father's house'.
and-to my-clan: 'and to' continues the verb 'go'.

phrases.english: and take a wife for my son
phrases.literal: and-you-take wife for-my-son: the weqatal continues the instruction.

grammar: אִם־לֹא opens the alternative: 'if not', i.e. the servant is to go to the father's house.
תֵּלֵךְ and וְלָקַחְתָּ are 2ms: the servant is addressed as 'you'.
בֵּית אָבִי: the father's household as the place of the bride's family.
segments.note: The 2ms verbs address the servant directly; the English 'you' keeps the number.
context: בֵּית אָב, 'father's house', is the household or extended family as a group, not only the single family; the English 'father's house' keeps the Hebrew.

segments.english: I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not go after me.'
segments.literal: and-I-said to my-master perhaps not she-goes the-woman after-me

tokens.note: The word is written without the vav (see apparatus).
Yiqtol 3fs: the subject is the woman.
Following: 'after me'.

phrases.literal: and-I-said to my-master: the speech is the servant's report of his own earlier words.

phrases.english: Perhaps the woman will not go after me
phrases.literal: perhaps not she-goes the-woman after-me: a fear, not a prohibition; the negative is with the yiqtol.

grammar: אֻלַי is the adverb 'perhaps', here without the vav.
לֹא תֵלֵךְ is a yiqtol 3fs with לֹא: the clause states a fear, 'perhaps she will not go'.
The speech is quoted as the servant's own words earlier; the English gives it in single quotes inside his speech.
segments.note: The written form lacks the vav; the English reads the word as 'perhaps'.

commentary.summary: Rashi reads the written אלי as 'to me' and tells that Eliezer had a daughter and sought a way for Abraham to speak to him of her marriage; Abraham answered that his son is blessed and Eliezer cursed. This is midrash; the English keeps 'perhaps', the plain sense of the word.

Radak: the vav is missing (defective spelling). A derash reads Eliezer's design into the word; he rejects it, holding that the speeches are reported as they were said, and that variant wording in repeated speeches keeps the same sense.

apparatus: Written without the vav (אֻלַי; the usual form is אוּלַי). Rashi reads the written form as 'to me'; Radak calls the spelling defective and keeps the same sense.

segments.english: He said to me, 'The LORD before whom I have walked will send his angel with you and will make your way prosper; and you shall take a wife for my son from my kin and from my father's house.'
segments.literal: and-he-said to-me the-LORD who I-walked-about before-him he-will-send his-angel with-you and-he-made-prosper your-way and-you-took wife for-my-son from-my-clan and-from-house-of my-father

tokens.note: Hitpael perfect 1cs: 'walk about' before him.
The angel is sent by the LORD: 'angel'.
The suffix is parsed as 2nd feminine singular; the addressee is a man, and English 'you' keeps the number and leaves the gender open.
Perfect with waw continuing the future of the clause.
Fig. for the course of the journey.
Perfect with waw continuing the instruction of 24:38.

phrases.literal: and-he-said to-me: Abraham speaks to the servant.

phrases.english: The LORD before whom I have walked
phrases.literal: the-LORD who I-walked-about before-him: the relative 'before whom' is the English for 'who' with 'before him'.

phrases.english: will send his angel with you
phrases.literal: he-will-send his-angel with-you: the angel is sent by the LORD.

phrases.english: and will make your way prosper
phrases.literal: and-he-made-prosper your-way: the perfect with waw continues the future; 'make prosper' is the causative.

phrases.english: and you shall take a wife for my son
phrases.literal: and-you-took wife for-my-son: the perfect with waw continues the instruction.

phrases.english: from my kin and from my father's house
phrases.literal: from-my-clan and-from-house-of my-father: the two sources of the wife.

grammar: The speech of Abraham is in single quotes inside the servant's speech; the outer double quotation stays open.
הִתְהַלַּכְתִּי is hitpael: 'walk about'; with לְפָנָיו it reads 'walk before him'.
The two future clauses: the LORD will send his angel and will make the way prosper; the second is a perfect with waw continuing the future.
The suffix on אִתָּךְ is parsed as 2nd feminine singular while the addressee is a man; the English 'you' keeps the number and leaves the gender open.
segments.note: The subject of the final instruction is 'you' (the servant), as in 24:38.
